sections.authorBiography: Charlotte Perkins Gilman was born in Hartford, Connecticut, on 3 July 1860, a relative of the Beecher family (Harriet Beecher Stowe was her great-aunt). After the birth of her daughter in 1885 she suffered severe depression and in 1887 was treated by the neurologist S. Weir Mitchell with his "rest cure," which forbade intellectual work; she later said it brought her near breakdown. She separated from her husband, moved to California and became a lecturer and writer on women's economic independence (Women and Economics, 1898) and author of the utopian story Herland (1915). Facing incurable cancer, she ended her life on 17 August 1935.
sections.historicalContext: In the nineteenth century, women with depression or "nervous" illness were often prescribed the "rest cure" of the neurologist S. Weir Mitchell: isolation, bed rest, overfeeding and a ban on intellectual work. Gilman underwent a version of it after the birth of her daughter in 1885. Married women had few legal rights, and doctors (usually men) had great authority over their patients.

publicationAndReception.publication: First published in The New England Magazine in January 1892. Gilman later said the editor of The Atlantic, Horace Scudder, rejected it, writing that he could not forgive himself if he made others as miserable as he had made himself.
publicationAndReception.then: Many readers read it as a horror story about madness; a Boston doctor protested that it could drive readers insane.
publicationAndReception.now: A foundational feminist text, rediscovered in the 1970s (the Feminist Press reissued it in 1973), and a classic of psychological horror and the unreliable narrator.

sections.overview: A young mother, taken by her physician husband John to a rented country house for a "rest cure," keeps a secret journal. She is forbidden to write and confined to a former nursery with hideous yellow wallpaper.
sections.whyItMatters: The story helped change how people thought about depression and women's autonomy, and it remains a powerful study of how silencing someone harms them.

spoilerOverview.text: She becomes convinced a woman is trapped behind the wallpaper's pattern, and in the end she tears it off, identifies with the trapped woman, and creeps around the room as her husband faints.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “John laughs at me, of course, but one expects that in marriage” slowly and put it in my own words: The narrator says her husband laughs at her, and adds that one expects that in marriage. Next, craft. I notice the tone is light, but "of course" and "one expects" show she has accepted being dismissed as normal. The strongest word is “laughs”: laughing is not cruelty exactly, but it refuses to take her seriously, which is the core problem in the story. Then, effect. What does this line show about the narrator's marriage? My answer: Gilman shows how a husband who controls his wife "for her own good" makes her fears seem silly; the casual tone hides a real lack of power.

segments.activity: Exit ticket on the author and context (answer given).
segments.script: Gilman was herself given the "rest cure" for depression in the 1880s. Why did she say she wrote this story? Answer: She wrote it to show the harm of the rest cure and to persuade doctors (including Dr. S. Weir Mitchell) to stop forbidding women all work and thought; accept answers that connect her own treatment to the story's purpose.

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this story, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in The Yellow Wallpaper.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about The Yellow Wallpaper: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

segments.activity: Students write to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Project the day's bell-ringer question (each lesson of The Yellow Wallpaper has its own). Students write silently for 5 minutes, then pair-share for 3. Call on one volunteer and one non-volunteer, and connect their answers to women and medical authority.

segments.activity: The day's key words in context, with verified word histories.
segments.script: Introduce the day's words in the sentences where they appear in The Yellow Wallpaper. Read each sentence aloud, ask students to guess the meaning from context, then give the gloss and the word history. Students copy one word into their journal with their own sentence.

Give the 10-minute background talk from the day's lesson: what happens in this story, the context a reader needs, and the literary elements to watch. Pause once to ask a check-for-understanding question.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud in the day's lesson.
segments.script: Read the anchor passage aloud twice. Model the three steps out loud: what the words say, what craft choice stands out and why, and what effect it has on the reader. The day's lesson gives the passage and a full written think-aloud.

segments.activity: Guided analysis of a second quotation; expected answers given.
segments.script: Display the second passage. Students annotate it in pairs using the same three steps; circulate, then take answers to the two guided questions and confirm them against the expected answers in the day's lesson.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Students annotate the story on their own (three marks with a margin note each) and write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph on the day's focus, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions, with facilitation notes.
segments.script: Run a 10-minute discussion from the day's anchor question and tiered questions. Start with literal checks, move to inference, and end with one evaluative question that ties the story to women and medical authority.

segments.activity: Story quiz in the app and an exit ticket (answer given).
segments.script: Students take the story quiz in the app, then answer the one-sentence exit ticket with a short quotation. Collect the tickets to plan the next lesson.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Restate the day's takeaway in one sentence, ask two students to name the line that best proves it, and preview the next reading in The Yellow Wallpaper.
